Ray Gun, premiere issue

The first issue of the music magazine Ray Gun, November 1992: painted and scratched covers, typewriter lists, and spreads where text is layered until it turns into texture.

Source
Display Graphic Design Collection: Ray Gun, Premiere Issue, November 1992
Creator
David Carson
Made
November 1992 (Display; Wikipedia)
Style
Grunge typography (agent-proposed, not yet reviewed by a person)
Moods
Raw, chaotic, dirty, intuitive
Evidence
Inspected eight photographs (1600 × 1279 each) of one copy offered by Display, a design collection and bookshop, in scratchpad copies: the cover, six interior spreads, and one further collaged page with the masthead. The copy has no collection number. Not stored.
Reviewed
28 September 2026
Rights
Link and metadata only. License: unverified. Rights policy

Context

Ray Gun was a music magazine first published in Santa Monica in 1992, with Marvin Scott Jarrett as publisher and David Carson as art director. Wikipedia describes its editorial pages as a “chaotic, abstract ‘grunge typography’ style”. Wikipedia).

Display lists the issue as no. 1, November 1992, 10 × 12 inches, 100 pages, with Carson credited as design consultant. Its first page reads “Raw by choice. Immediate by necessity. Alternative by design.” Display.

Features include Henry Rollins, Sonic Youth (photographed by Spike Jonze), The Lemonheads, and The Prodigy. Display.

Observed

  • The cover is a scraped yellow, white, and black painted surface with pencil scrawl, paint spatter, and a heavy black scribble.
  • Two black-and-white face fragments are cut into rough rectangles and pasted into the paint.
  • The masthead “rAY GUn” is a red condensed sans-serif in mixed case, with letters of different heights; “PREMIERE ISSUE” is blue hand lettering; the band list is a typewriter face, indented in an uneven zigzag.
  • The Sonic Youth opener layers strips of contact-sheet film, overprinted serif and sans-serif lines, and blue text until lines collide.
  • A second Sonic Youth spread has large blue hand-painted words over a page of body text, facing a painted face on red gingham with a scrawled title.
  • One spread overprints lines of text in several faces until the headline area becomes a solid black mass.
  • A music-video feature sets its body in a condensed typewriter face, justified in narrow columns, facing a cropped blue duotone photograph.
  • Headlines break words across lines and space them down the page (“lov / i / ng / the / rock / star”).

Why it belongs

The issue shows the whole grammar at once: damaged grounds, several unrelated faces per spread, and body text used as a texture. The typewriter lists and captions are the stable voice among the noise.

Borrow

Set a list of names in a typewriter face with alternating indents instead of a clean column.

Overprint a headline in several faces and colors until part of it becomes a black mass, and keep the body text clean beside it.

Paste photo fragments with rough rectangular edges onto a painted or scratched ground.

A growing catalogue of visual references. Rights and removal
